title: A "Faster Horse" Isn't a Solution: Why Legacy Martech Is Falling Behind B2C Enterprises
summary: Discover why legacy martech is failing B2C enterprises in ANZ & SEA, and why agile, high-speed platforms are essential for driving growth without friction
body_markdown:
Why B2C Martech Needs More Agility


Generated by Klaviyo AI


Legacy martech platforms often prioritise complexity and governance at the expense of speed, usability, and adoption. B2C enterprises increasingly need scalable systems that support real-time activation, rapid experimentation, cross-channel execution, and measurable growth.


-


**Complexity creates friction:** Campaign delays, fragmented data, and slow reporting prevent teams from responding quickly to customer demand.


-


**Speed drives relevance:** Modern B2C teams need to test, learn, and activate customer insights continuously rather than follow fixed campaign calendars.


-


**Simplicity improves adoption:** Tools that teams use consistently can produce better data and outcomes than powerful platforms that are difficult to operate.

---


If you run marketing for a B2C enterprise, you already know the tension: your business is moving fast, your customers are moving faster, and your tech stack still moves at the pace of a procurement committee. That gap is starting to show.


Enterprise marketing platforms were built to serve the biggest, most complex organisations with more features, more governance, and more layers of control. None of that is inherently bad; much of it was genuinely necessary. But when a platform is optimised for complexity instead of speed, something backfires: the teams who most need to move fast end up slowed down by the very systems meant to support them.


This is where Clayton Christensen's theory of disruption is useful. Disruption happens when a market long served by incumbents gets challenged by tools that are simpler, faster to adopt, and more closely aligned with how people actually work. In martech, legacy platforms spent years adding features to satisfy their most demanding customers - a classic approach to sustaining innovation. But underneath that complexity, a different kind of platform has been emerging: one built around usability, speed, and direct action.


Early on, these newer tools can look less "enterprise-grade." That's often the point. The market no longer rewards the most complicated stack, it rewards the one that helps teams act, learn, and scale without friction.


For B2C enterprises, this isn't a future trend. It's already underway.


Across ANZ and South East Asia, brands are winning more customers than ever while owning fewer of those relationships. Australian households now buy from an average of 16 different brands a year, make four more online purchases than they did last year, and spend less each time, with the average basket size falling to $96. In South East Asia, video commerce has grown from marginal to a quarter of all ecommerce GMV in three years, and that growth arrives on someone else's platform. In both markets: more purchases, more brands, smaller baskets. Unless those relationships are captured somewhere brands own, they are renting an audience they think they've bought.


## Why legacy stacks are starting to struggle


Disruption doesn't happen just because a new tool looks shiny. It happens when the conditions are finally in place. For B2C enterprises, those conditions are visible right now:


Customers move faster than internal systems. Consumers shift between channels and devices in real time. If your stack can't keep pace, the experience breaks down.


Growth teams need activation, not quarterly reports. Marketing today is a performance engine; testing, learning, and iterating continuously, not running campaigns on a calendar.


Simplicity drives adoption. A tool people actually use consistently produces better data and better outcomes than a powerful one that is difficult to use.


Complexity has become a cost, not a credential. Gartner found martech utilisation fell to 49% in 2025, down from 56% the year before, and named complexity and sprawl of the current stack as the single biggest obstacle.


## Time to stop building the "faster horse"


The "faster horse" line, usually attributed to Henry Ford, captures why customers often ask for a better version of what they already have when what they actually need is a different approach entirely.


In martech, the faster-horse instinct looks like more features, more controls, more governance. It sounds robust. It feels safe. But it often just makes the system harder to use and slower to move.


That's exactly where disruption takes hold. Legacy platforms won't disappear overnight; they'll simply lose relevance where speed and usability matter as much as scalability. The new generation of tools isn't "less enterprise." It's more useful to the people actually driving growth. That's a different bar, and it's one a lot of legacy systems aren't clearing anymore.


## What a resilient B2C stack needs to do


B2C enterprises don't just need marketing tools, they need systems that can keep pace with customer demand, channel complexity, and constant experimentation. That means a stack built for:


- Rapid campaign iteration
- Real-time data activation
- Cross-channel orchestration
- Measurable ROI across acquisition and retention
- Faster decisions across marketing, CRM, and ecommerce
- Yet still scalable for growing enterprise businesses


Legacy stacks were built around process. They scale well, but they rarely feel agile, and in B2C marketing today, agility isn't a nice-to-have, it's the difference between capturing demand and watching it walk away.


The familiar symptoms show up everywhere: campaigns delayed by IT, teams working around the platform instead of with it, customer data fragmented across systems, and reporting too slow to inform real decisions.


The businesses winning right now are free to connect customer insight, creative execution, and channel activation in a way that feels fast and coordinated. That takes a different stack, and a different mindset: one built around velocity and simplicity.


## What that looks like in practice


The strongest B2C teams aren't chasing more complexity, they're chasing more leverage. That means choosing tools that are:


- Easy enough for teams to adopt consistently
- Built for real-time engagement
- Connected enough to support omnichannel execution
- Flexible enough for experimentation without friction
- Designed to help marketers act, not just report


In this environment enterprise-grade doesn't have to mean enterprise-heavy. The goal is to be scalable while ensuring there’s less friction, so teams can move faster and decide smarter with the data they already have.


## One final thought…


Christensen's theory is a useful reminder that markets shift before incumbents are ready to admit it. For B2C enterprise teams, that shift already shows up in the pressure to move faster, personalise more deeply, and prove ROI on every interaction.


If your stack is built for governance more than growth, you are dealing with more friction and running a slower, less responsive revenue engine.


The disruption isn't coming. It's already reshaping how customer-facing teams compete. The brands that choose speed, clarity, and direct customer value over legacy complexity will be the ones that move first - and the ones that win.
